unit.title: Assist in the provision of on the job training

summary: This unit prepares you, as an experienced Level 3 welder, to help train apprentices and new workers on the job. You will learn what a workplace trainer does and where the role stops, how to find out what a trainee can already do, how to plan training around real work, how to keep trainees safe, how to explain and demonstrate a task, how to supervise practice and give feedback that helps, and how to check, record and report progress and judge whether the training worked.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). In most Jamaican fabrication shops, apprentices and new workers learn the trade beside experienced welders. This unit is about doing that well: helping a trainee become safe, skilled and confident, without taking over the job of the supervisor or the assessor.

A good workplace trainer saves the shop money and injuries. Trainees who are shown the right way, and told why, make fewer faults, waste less steel and stay safer. Trainees left to 'pick it up' copy every bad habit around them.
**Who it is for:** Welding Level 3 trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and experienced welders asked to coach apprentices, new hires or trainees on work experience.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the shop
rows: Understand your role
Know what the workplace trainer, mentor, supervisor, training officer and assessor each do, and where your part stops.
Set a good example
Work safely and to the standard every time, because trainees copy what they see.
Find out training needs
Find out what a trainee can already do, compare it with the unit standards and the shop's work, and list the gaps in order.
Plan the training
Write clear objectives, put the skills in a sensible order, use real jobs, prepare the place, equipment and materials, and agree the plan.
Keep trainees safe
Induct them, check their PPE, supervise closely, and stop unsafe acts at once.
Explain and demonstrate
Explain the task and the reasons for each step, demonstrate so the trainee can see safely, and break long tasks into stages.
Supervise practice and give feedback
Watch closely, correct at once, let the trainee try again, find the causes of repeated faults, and give clear, specific feedback.
Check, record and report progress
Judge progress against the standard with sound evidence, keep honest training records, and report to the supervisor.
Evaluate the training
Find out whether the training worked, and use the lessons to improve the next plan.

ul: A **multiple-choice paper** on the trainer's role, training needs, planning, safety, demonstrating, practice, feedback, checking progress, records and evaluation, with a few simple sums on hours and pass rates.

A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms (mentor, assessor, induction, coupon, portfolio, apprenticeship, WPS, undercut, visual inspection) and sums; and longer answers in full sentences, for example how you would demonstrate a fillet weld or give feedback on a poor weld.

**Practical tasks** done as a group: plan, demonstrate and coach a horizontal fillet weld (2F), with each member both teaching and being taught; and a skills check on oxy-fuel cutting, a two-week training plan for an apprentice and a progress review role play.

blocks.note: In the practicals you are marked as a trainer as well as a welder: a clear explanation, a demonstration the trainee can see safely, close watching, stepping in at once on any unsafe act, checking understanding, and feedback with one good point and one or two specific points to improve.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: An apprentice learns most of the trade at work, from the people around them. Several people share the training, and each has a different part.

head: Person
Their part in the training
rows: Apprentice or trainee
Learns, practises, asks questions, works safely, keeps the logbook up to date
Workplace trainer (you)
Helps find the trainee's needs, plans with the supervisor, prepares, explains and demonstrates, supervises practice, gives feedback, checks progress, keeps records and reports
Mentor
An experienced worker who advises the apprentice over a long period on the trade, good work habits and getting on at work; often, but not always, the same person as the trainer
Supervisor
Agrees the training plan, sets aside time and resources for it, and decides what work the trainee may do
Training officer or training centre
Keeps the programme on track and links the workplace with the centre
Assessor
A qualified person who makes the formal judgement of competence against the unit standard

blocks.note: Your role stops at coaching, checking and reporting. You do not sign anyone off as competent for a qualification: a qualified assessor does that, using evidence. Your honest records and observations are part of that evidence.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: An **apprenticeship** is a formal period, under an agreement with an employer, in which a person learns a trade while working. In Jamaica, HEART/NSTA Trust runs apprenticeship and workplace training programmes, and NCTVET awards the national vocational qualifications (NVQ-J). Each qualification is made of **unit standards**, which say what a competent worker must be able to do, and to what standard.
**Competent** means the trainee can do the task safely, to the standard, without help, every time, in the conditions of real work. One good weld on a good day is not competence.

ul: Trainees copy what they see far more than what they are told. If you chip slag without glasses, they will too.
Wear full PPE, follow the WPS, keep your bay tidy, store electrodes properly and report faults, every time, especially when trainees are watching.
Speak to trainees with respect, be on time, admit your own mistakes, and ask for help when you need it.
Give every trainee the same tasks, chances and respect, whatever their sex, background or age.
Provide lifting aids and team lifts for heavy work for everyone, rather than keeping some people off it.
Do not allow teasing, bullying or remarks that a trade task is 'not for' a certain kind of person; challenge them and report them if they continue.
Make reasonable changes for a disability where the work can still be done safely, after talking to the trainee and the supervisor.

blocks.p: People learn at different speeds and in different ways. Some like to see a thing done (visual), some to hear it explained and talk it through (auditory or aural), some to handle it and try it (kinaesthetic, or hands-on). Most people learn a practical trade best from a mix: hear the reason, see it done, do it with feedback, and do it again.

ul: Explain why, not only how: people remember steps they understand.
Link each skill to real jobs in the shop.
Teach in small steps, with practice soon after each one.
Praise real progress, honestly and specifically.
If a trainee is not progressing, change the approach: another explanation, more guided practice, smaller steps.

blocks.p: A **training needs analysis** compares what a trainee can do now with what the unit standards and the shop's work require. The difference, the **gap**, is the training need.

flow: Talk with the trainee: schooling, any welding or metalwork done before, certificates, what they want to learn
Watch them do simple tasks safely on scrap: set up a booth, strike an arc and run beads, mark out and cut, use a grinder
Ask them to explain the steps and the hazards, to check understanding
Compare what you saw with the unit standards and with the shop's usual work
List the gaps in order: safety first, then the basic skills that later skills build on
Agree the list with the trainee and the supervisor, and record it

blocks.note: What a trainee can show you on scrap tells you far more than what they say about themselves. Ten minutes of watching shows how they hold a grinder, set a machine and control an arc, and mistakes on scrap cost almost nothing.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Skill
What you saw
Training need
Order
rows: Shop safety
Did not know where the gas shut-off or the extinguishers are
Full induction
Grinding
Held the grinder in one hand; no face shield
Safe grinding method, with checks
PPE
Gloves worn through; no glasses under the helmet
New gloves; daily PPE check for the first weeks
Flat MMAW beads
Steady arc, but uneven travel speed
Stringer bead practice
Reading a WPS
Struggles with the written terms
Go through real WPSs with sketches
Horizontal fillet (2F)
Not tried
Tee and lap fillet welds
Vertical-up fillet (3F)
Not tried
After 2F is steady

blocks.p: Use the shop's own work to decide what matters most. If most jobs are gates and fences in thin-wall square tube, then fit-up and welding of tube come before heavy plate. If the shop does coded structural work, the trainee needs to learn to follow a WPS exactly.
A training objective says what the trainee will do, under what conditions, and to what standard. It must be clear enough that you and the trainee can both tell whether it has been met.

head: Too loose
Clear and checkable
rows: Learn about fillet welds
Weld a single-pass horizontal fillet (2F) on 8 mm plate with 3.2 mm E6013 to the WPS, legs 6 ± 1 mm, with no undercut or slag on the surface, without help
Understand gas cutting
Set up, leak-test, light and shut down an oxy-acetylene set safely, and cut 10 mm plate within 2 mm of a marked line, unaided

flow: Induction, PPE and shop safety
Hand tools, measuring and marking out
Grinding and cutting
Setting up the welding machine
Tacking and fit-up
Beads, then fillet welds in the flat and horizontal positions
Butt welds
Vertical, then overhead, then pipe

blocks.p: Each skill builds on the one before: a trainee cannot make a good fillet weld on a joint they cannot cut, fit and tack. Teach simple before complex, and safe habits before speed.

ul: Practise first on offcuts of the **same material and joint** as the real work, until the welds pass.
Then let the trainee do parts of real jobs under close supervision, starting with less critical parts.
Real jobs teach working to a real standard and a real deadline, and keep the trainee interested.
Never put a trainee on work that needs a qualified welder, such as coded work to a WPS they are not qualified for.

head: Question
Working
Answer
rows: A trainee needs 90 hours of supervised practice and gets 6 hours a week
15 weeks
Training is 20% of a 40-hour week
8 hours a week
You supervise 2 trainees for 3 hours and 4 trainees for 2 hours
14 trainee-hours

ul: The trainee's name, start date and the needs found
The objectives, and the tasks in order
Who trains each task, when and for how long
The safety points and the resources needed
How progress will be checked, and the review dates
Signatures: the plan is agreed with the **supervisor** and the **trainee** before you use it

blocks.p: A **session plan** sets out one training session: the objective, the place and resources, the safety points, the steps and key points, the time for demonstration, practice and questions, how the result will be checked, and the record to fill in. Before the session, check:

ul: The booth is screened, clear and dry; the extraction works.
The machine, leads, holder and clamp are in good order.
PPE for the trainee and for anyone watching: helmet with the right shade, safety glasses, gloves, jacket, boots.
Plate offcuts cut and cleaned; electrodes or wire as the WPS says, dry; tools and a weld gauge to hand.
The WPS or job sheet; an extinguisher; and time free of production work.

blocks.p: Keep the group small enough that you can watch each trainee's every run. Never have more trainees welding than there are booths. If you are asked to supervise more trainees than you can safely watch, explain the risk to your supervisor and agree smaller groups or a rota.

blocks.note: Many small shops train while working to tight deadlines, and training time is the first thing to be dropped. Agree with the supervisor, in the plan, which hours are set aside for training, and report it when production keeps taking them.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: New workers are hurt far more often than experienced ones: they do not yet see the hazards. Safety comes before any skill.

A trainee's first session is an **induction**: the shop rules; exits and the assembly point; fire extinguishers and how to raise the alarm; the first-aid kit and first aiders; the gas shut-off valves and the main electrical isolator; the main hazards; PPE; how to report accidents and near misses; and whom to ask.

head: Hazard for trainees
Control
rows: Arc light while watching
Helmet down with the right shade, or a screen; watchers stand beside the trainer, never behind an open screen
Fume
Extraction close to the arc; coatings removed from galvanised or painted steel; a respirator where the risk assessment says
Hot metal
Treat all metal as hot; tongs; mark hot work
Grinders, saws, shears, plasma cutters
Used only after training and sign-off; guards on; discs of the right type and speed rating
Gas cylinders
Upright and chained; valves closed at the end of the day; flashback arrestors fitted; no oil or grease on oxygen fittings
Fire
Anything that burns cleared away; extinguisher at hand
Noise
Ear protection; instructions given away from the noise
Heavy plate and sections
Lifting aids or team lifts

ul: Cylinders upright and chained or strapped, so they cannot fall and break a valve.
Regulators, hoses and fittings checked before use; flashback arrestors in place.
Leak-test every joint with leak-detection solution, never with a flame: a leak shows as bubbles.
Open cylinder valves slowly; light and shut down in the order the maker and the Centre's procedure give.
Never use oxygen to blow dust off clothing or to cool yourself. Clothing soaked with oxygen catches fire easily and burns fiercely.

blocks.note: Take lighters and matches out of your pockets before welding or cutting, and teach trainees to do the same. Hot slag or a spark can make a lighter burst into flame against your body.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: When you see an unsafe act

flow: Stop the work at once; switch off or isolate if needed
Explain calmly why it is dangerous
Show the safe way
Let the trainee do it again while you watch
Record it, and report serious or repeated breaches to the supervisor
Check whether other trainees have picked up the same habit

blocks.p: If a trainee keeps making the same safety mistake, such as leaving cylinder valves open at the end of the day, report it, retrain, and check every day until the habit is fixed. Do not quietly do it for them.

blocks.h: First aid for common training injuries

head: Injury
What to do
rows: Burn

Cool under cool running water for about 20 minutes; remove rings or watches near the burn; do not burst blisters or put on ice, butter or grease; cover loosely with a clean, non-fluffy dressing or cling film; get medical help for large or deep burns; report it
Speck in the eye
Do not rub; rinse with clean water or sterile eyewash; if it will not wash out, or is stuck in the eye, cover the eye and get medical help; report it
Arc eye
Do not rub; see a doctor or nurse; report it
Electric shock
Switch off before touching the person; call 110; give CPR if you are trained and it is needed; report it

blocks.note: Record every injury and near miss, however small, and tell the supervisor. Records show where training or equipment needs to change.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Step
What you do
Why
rows: 1 Explain
In a quiet place, say what the task is, what the finished job must look like, the key points and hazards, and **why** each key point matters
People remember steps they understand, and can apply them to new jobs
2 Demonstrate
Do the task once at normal speed, then again slowly, naming each key point; the trainee watches safely from where they can see
Seeing it done right gives the picture to copy
3 Practise
The trainee does it while you watch closely; correct at once; repeat until the result is steady
Skill comes from doing, with correction
4 Check
Inspect the result together; ask the trainee to explain why; record it; check again on later jobs
Confirms the skill and the understanding, and shows what comes next

blocks.p: Under a helmet, a trainee sees little but the bright arc unless placed well. Have them stand or sit beside you, at about the same distance from the arc as your eyes, with their helmet down and the same filter shade. With more than one watcher, demonstrate a short run for each in turn. Never let anyone look at the arc without a filter, even 'for a second'.

blocks.h: Breaking a long task into stages

blocks.p: A long procedure is taught in stages, each practised before the next. For example, setting up a TIG set for mild steel:

ol: Gas: cylinder chained; argon regulator and flowmeter fitted; hose checked.
Torch: the right tungsten, ground to a point lengthwise; collet, collet body and cup fitted.
Machine: DC, electrode negative; current and post-flow set as the WPS says.
Gas flow set and checked at the torch.
Test run on scrap, then adjust.

head: Key point
The reason to give
rows: Clean mill scale, rust, paint and oil off the joint
They cause porosity, slag inclusions and poor fusion
Tack both ends and check square before welding
The weld shrinks as it cools and pulls the parts out of line
Keep a short arc
A long arc lets air in (porosity), spatters and undercuts
Take low-hydrogen electrodes from the oven only as needed
Damp flux puts hydrogen into the weld, causing porosity and cracking
Fill the crater at the end of a run
An unfilled crater can crack

blocks.h: Example: demonstrating a vertical-up fillet weld (3F) with MMAW

head: Key point
What to show (typical; follow the WPS)
rows: Electrode and current
Usually 3.2 mm; current lower than for the same fillet in the horizontal position, often by about 10–20%, within the packet's range and the WPS
Electrode angle
Halfway between the plates (about 45°), pointing slightly upwards, about 5–15° above square to the joint
Arc and pool
A short arc and a small pool, so the metal does not sag
Movement
A small triangular or side-to-side weave, pausing at each toe to fill it, moving up steadily
Faults to watch for
Sagging metal (too hot or too slow), undercut at the toes (no pause at the edges or too much current), trapped slag (weave too wide)

blocks.p: Teach the proper names for faults and weld parts: porosity, undercut, overlap, lack of fusion, slag inclusion, crater crack, spatter, toe, root, leg length, throat. A trainee who can name a fault can look up its causes and report it clearly; 'bad weld' tells nobody anything.

ul: Do not ask 'Do you understand?': most people say yes.
Ask the trainee to show the step and explain it, or ask 'what if' questions: 'Why did you set 115 A?' 'What would you change if the bead sagged?'

For a trainee who finds reading hard, go through the WPS with them, with sketches and the real joint in front of you, and mark the key figures. Do it privately, never in front of others, and never skip the WPS.

blocks.note: In a noisy shop, step away from the noise or stop the noisy work nearby, and speak face to face. Agree a clear hand signal for 'stop'. Never lift a trainee's ear defenders while grinders are running.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Stay close and watch each run from the start; you cannot coach what you did not see.
Step in at once if the trainee is unsafe or a bad habit is forming (a long arc, a wrong angle): stop them, show the right way, and let them try again.
Do not take the holder and finish the weld yourself, and do not save the correction for next week.
Let the trainee repeat until the result is right every time, then move on to a harder joint or position.
Practise on coupons first; test pieces for assessment come only when the practice welds are steady.

blocks.h: Finding the cause of a repeated fault

blocks.p: When a fault keeps coming back, do not just say 'try harder'. Watch the whole process, check the likely causes one at a time, and ask the trainee what they think the cause is.

head: Fault
Causes to check
Coaching point
rows: Porosity
Dirty or wet plate; damp electrodes; long arc; draughts; low gas flow, blocked nozzle or leaking hose (MIG and TIG)
Clean to bright metal; dry electrodes; short arc; screens; check the gas
Undercut
Current too high; arc too long; travel too fast; wrong angle; no pause at the toes
Less current; shorter arc; pause at the edges
Uneven fillet legs
Electrode not halfway between the plates; pool too big and sagging onto the lower plate
Aim at the root at about 45°; a smaller pool
Heavy spatter
Long arc; current too high; damp electrodes; wrong polarity
Short arc; check the setting and the polarity
Slag inclusions
Slag not removed between runs; weave too wide; slag running ahead of the pool
Clean every run; tighter weave; correct angle
Lack of fusion
Current too low; travel too fast; arc playing on the pool instead of the plate edges
More current; slower travel; aim at the edges
Burn-through on thin metal
Current too high; gap too wide; travel too slow
Less current; tighter fit-up; shorter runs

head: Do
Why it matters
rows: Give it soon after the task, in a quiet place, in private
It is fresh in the trainee's mind, and they are not shamed in front of others
Ask first: 'How do you think it went?'
Trainees learn more from faults they spot themselves
Start with something done well, honestly
They keep doing it, and they listen to the rest
Give one or two specific points, each with its cause and fix
Too many points at once confuse and discourage; specific points can be acted on
Use trade words and measurements
'The upper leg is 5 mm and the lower 8 mm' is clearer than 'bad weld'
Never belittle
Remarks such as 'you should know that by now' stop people learning
Ask the trainee to say what they will change; watch the next attempt; record it
Checks understanding and shows progress

blocks.note: Example of feedback on an open-root butt weld: 'Your restart is well fused and the cap is straight: keep doing that. The root has not come through along the last 60 mm. Watch the keyhole: it got smaller as you sped up near the end. Keep the same speed and the same size of keyhole all the way. Tell me what you'll watch for on the next one.'
blocks.label: Tip

head: Evidence
What it shows
rows: Visual inspection with gauges
Size, profile and surface faults: undercut, porosity, cracks, overlap, spatter
Bend test
A strip cut across a practice weld (a **coupon**) is bent round a former; lack of fusion, inclusions and porosity inside the weld open up as cracks or tears
Macro (etch) test
A cut cross-section is ground smooth and etched, showing penetration, fusion and inclusions; done by a trained person, as the etching acid is dangerous
Observation
The trainee does the whole task unaided, safely, on several occasions, on real work: the strongest sign of competence
Questioning
Whether the trainee understands why, and what to do when conditions change
Records
Signed task sheets, logbook entries and photos that show progress over time

blocks.p: Competence means right, unaided, safe, every time, on real work. A trainee saying they feel confident, having watched you many times, or passing a written test does not show it on its own.
A good record entry lets anyone see what was done, to what standard, and what comes next.

head: Poor entry
Good entry
rows: 'Welding OK this week.'
'10 Nov 2026. 3F fillet, 10 mm plate, E7018 3.2 mm, WPS-07. Visual: legs 8 mm, no undercut; one restart not fused. Next: practise restarts. Signed: trainer / apprentice.'

ul: Write entries on the day, from what you saw. Never write entries from memory weeks later, and never sign for a task that was not done, even to keep the plan on track.
Keep failed coupons and record them too: honest records show the faults that were worked on and how the trainee improved.
Photograph bent and etched coupons with their identity mark and the date, and keep the photos with the record.

blocks.p: A **portfolio** (portfolio of evidence) is the collection of evidence, such as photos, signed task sheets, test results and logbook pages, that shows what the trainee can do. The assessor uses it, with observation and questioning, to judge competence.

head: Question
Working
Answer
rows: 14 of 16 practice coupons passed the bend test
Pass rate rose from 9 of 20 to 17 of 20

ul: Report progress to the supervisor regularly, with evidence.
Report problems early: training time lost to production, repeated safety lapses, a trainee who is struggling or often absent.

When asked whether a trainee can work with less supervision, watch the whole task done unaided more than once, check the welds by eye and by test, check safe working every time, ask questions, and then report what you saw, with the records.

blocks.p: Evaluation asks: did the training work, and was it worth the time? A trainee who enjoyed a session, or a session that finished on time, does not prove that anyone learned anything. Look at four levels:

head: Level
Question
Evidence
rows: Reaction
Did the trainee find it useful?
Ask the trainee
Learning
Can the trainee now do and explain the task?
Coupons, tests, questions
Work
Does the trainee do it right on real jobs without help?
Observation; the supervisor's and other welders' views
Results
Has the shop gained?
Fewer rejects and less re-work, time saved, fewer injuries

flow: Start from the objectives in the training plan
Gather evidence from the trainee's work: tests, unaided tasks, safe working
Compare the first records with the latest ones to show the progress
Ask the trainee, the supervisor and other welders for their views
Check time and cost: were the sessions held as planned?
Write a short report: results, gaps still left, and suggestions
Change the next training plan to use the lessons

blocks.note: When one trainee progresses well and another does not, look at the training as well as the trainee. The slower one may need a different explanation, more hands-on guided practice, shorter steps, or help with reading, rather than more of the same.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say 'I can' to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can describe the parts played by the trainee, workplace trainer, mentor, supervisor, training officer and assessor, and say where my role stops.
I can explain what competence means, and why a trainer's example matters.
I can treat every trainee fairly and adapt to how each one learns.
I can carry out a training needs analysis and list the gaps in a sensible order.
I can write clear, checkable training objectives.
I can order skills from simple to complex and plan training around real work.
I can work out training hours, weeks and trainee-hours.
I can write a training plan and a session plan, and prepare a session.
I can induct a trainee and control the hazards of training in a working shop.
I can teach gas safety, including leak testing and the danger of oxygen on clothing.
I can stop an unsafe act and correct it, and give first aid for common training injuries.
I can explain, demonstrate, supervise practice and check, using the four-step method.
I can let a trainee watch a weld safely and see what I see.
I can find the cause of a repeated weld fault and coach the fix.
I can give specific, helpful feedback.
I can judge progress with sound evidence and keep honest training records.
I can evaluate training and report on whether it worked.

terms: A formal period, under an agreement with an employer, of learning a trade while working
A qualified person who makes the formal judgement of competence against the standard
A test in which a strip cut from a weld is bent to show faults inside it
Able to do a task safely, to the standard, without help, every time, at work
A test piece, or a strip cut from a test weld, used for testing
Information given to a trainee about how they did and how to improve
A safety device on a gas set that stops a flame travelling back into the hose and cylinder
The first session for a new worker: rules, hazards, exits, first aid and emergency points
A liquid brushed onto gas joints; a leak shows as bubbles
Examining a cut, smoothed and etched cross-section of a weld
An experienced worker who advises an apprentice over a long period
A statement of what the trainee will do, under what conditions, to what standard
The collection of evidence that shows what a trainee can do
The plan for one training session
Comparing what a trainee can do with what is needed, to find the gap
The agreed plan of a trainee's training: needs, objectives, tasks, times, trainers and checks
The statement of what a competent worker must do in one unit of a qualification, and to what standard
Checking a weld by eye, with gauges, for size, shape and surface faults
Welding procedure specification: the process, consumables, settings and preparation for a weld

c1.title: Two new starters in Falmouth
c1.text: Garfield Reid, a Level 3 welder at a fabrication shop in Falmouth, Trelawny, is asked by his supervisor to help train two new starters. Odane, 19, has a school certificate in welding and wants to start on the shop's jobs at once; on scrap plate his arc is steady, but he grinds holding the grinder in one hand, with no face shield. Shanelle, 22, has never welded. Next month the shop starts a contract for 60 fence panels in thin-wall square tube.

c2.title: Vertical-up practice in Santa Cruz
c2.text: At a steel shop in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth, Desmond Brooks is coaching an apprentice, Rushane, on vertical-up fillet welds (3F) with 3.2 mm E7018 electrodes. The WPS gives 90–115 A for this joint. Rushane's coupons sag in the middle and show undercut at both toes. Desmond finds the machine set at 135 A, and sees that Rushane weaves straight across the joint without stopping at the edges.

c3.title: Oxy-fuel cutting in a yard in Hayes
c3.text: Sophia Wynter, a Level 3 welder at a shop in Hayes, Clarendon, is supervising three apprentices cutting plate with oxy-acetylene in the yard. During the morning she sees Jovan using the oxygen hose to blow dust off his overalls, an acetylene cylinder standing loose against a post, and Dorian cutting with a disposable lighter in his shirt pocket. Later, a speck of grinding dust gets into Jovan's eye.

c4.title: Getting a portfolio ready in Linstead
c4.text: Collin Bryan has trained an apprentice, Kimoy, for four months at a shop in Linstead, St Catherine. Her assessor will visit next month to look at her portfolio. Collin finds that her logbook has no entries for three weeks, although she says she did 'plenty of 2G practice'. This month she bent 16 practice coupons and 13 passed; she threw the three that failed into the scrap bin. She asks Collin to sign her 2G unit as 'competent' so that she can finish sooner.

c5.title: Three months of training in Port Antonio
c5.text: Trevor Samuels has coached two apprentices, Jody-Ann and Akeem, for three months at a fabrication and boat-repair shop in Port Antonio, Portland. Jody-Ann's bend-test pass rate has risen from 40% to 85%. Akeem's has risen only from 45% to 55%; he often asks to be shown again, and his welds improve most when Trevor guides his hand position during practice. The owner, Mr Duhaney, asks whether the training has paid off.

questions.q: What should come first in Odane's training, before he does any more work?
o: Fillet welds in square tube, since the fence contract starts next month
Safe grinding: two hands on the grinder, guard set and a face shield on
Vertical-up welding, as his flat beads are already steady on scrap
Reading the fence drawings, so that he can start cutting the panels
questions.why: Safety gaps come before any skill. One-handed grinding without a face shield can cost him an eye or a hand, however steady his arc is. Once that is fixed, he moves on to the welding skills the contract needs.

questions.q: Odane wants to start on the fence panels at once. What practice should come first?
o: Practice on 10 mm plate, which is harder, so the tube will seem easy
Weld the first few panels, then repair any of them that fail the check
Watch Garfield weld the first ten panels, then carry on from there
Practice on offcuts of the same tube and joint until his welds pass
questions.why: Thin-wall tube burns through and distorts easily, so skill on thick plate does not carry straight over. Practising on offcuts of the same tube and joint costs little and shows when he is ready for the real panels.

questions.q: Shanelle needs about 66 hours of supervised practice before she can tack the panels. She gets 1.5 hours a day, 4 days a week. How many weeks will it take?
o: 11 weeks
44 weeks
16.5 weeks
9 weeks
questions.why: She gets 1.5 × 4 = 6 hours a week, and 66 ÷ 6 = 11 weeks. Dividing by the daily figure alone (66 ÷ 1.5 = 44) gives days, not weeks.

questions.q: What explains both the sagging and the undercut on Rushane's coupons?
o: The electrodes are damp, so the arc is spattering
Too much heat: the current is above the WPS range
The plates were not cleaned before they were tacked
The electrode is too small for a vertical fillet
questions.why: At 135 A he is well above the 90–115 A the WPS gives, so the pool is too big and runs down (sagging), and the edges melt away (undercut). Bring the current into the range first.

questions.q: With the current corrected, what should Desmond show Rushane about his weave?
o: Weave faster and much wider, so that the pool cannot build up in the middle
Stop weaving and run straight up the joint as a single stringer bead
Pause briefly at each toe, so the edges fill, and cross the middle faster
Hold a longer arc, so that the heat spreads out to both edges
questions.why: A short pause at each toe fills the edge and stops undercut; crossing the middle quickly stops the centre building up and sagging. A longer arc would make the undercut and spatter worse.

questions.q: Which is the best way for Desmond to open his feedback to Rushane?
o: List every fault he can see on the coupons, so none is missed
Tell him that the coupons are bad and that he must try again
Show the other apprentices the coupons as an example of faults
Ask Rushane how he thinks the coupons went and what he noticed
questions.why: Asking first gets the trainee thinking, and he learns more from faults he spots himself. Desmond then names something done well and gives one or two specific points. Long lists and public criticism discourage.

questions.q: Why should Rushane take the E7018 electrodes from the holding oven only as he needs them?
o: So he does not lose count of how many electrodes he has used
Because a warm electrode is much easier to strike than a cold one
The flux takes up moisture, which can cause porosity and cracking
So that the oven door is not left open while he is in the booth
questions.why: E7018 is a low-hydrogen electrode. Its flux soaks up moisture from humid air, and the moisture puts hydrogen into the weld, causing porosity and cracking. That is the reason a trainee should be given, not only the rule.

questions.q: Why must Sophia stop Jovan at once?
o: Clothing soaked with oxygen catches fire easily and burns fiercely
Oxygen is a poisonous gas, and he may breathe some of it in
It wastes the oxygen that the shop has paid for and needs for cutting
The dust can explode like flour when oxygen is blown through it
questions.why: Oxygen stays in cloth for some time, and a single spark can then set the clothing alight in a fierce fire. Brush dust off clothing; never use oxygen, or compressed air, on clothes or skin.

questions.q: What should be done about the loose acetylene cylinder?
o: Lay it down flat on the ground, where it cannot fall over again
Stand it upright and chain or strap it before work goes on
Leave it as it is, as long as nobody is working near it
Move it into the sun so that the gas pressure stays even
questions.why: A falling cylinder can break its valve or regulator and release gas. Acetylene cylinders must stand upright, because the acetone inside them must not reach the valve, and they are kept away from heat.

questions.q: Why must Dorian take the lighter out of his shirt pocket?
o: It may fall out and get lost in the scrap pile
Its gas could put out the cutting flame
Slag or a spark can make it burst into flame
Its metal parts may set off the gas regulator
questions.why: A spark or a piece of hot slag can melt a disposable lighter and make it burst into flame against his body. Lighters and matches come out of pockets before any hot work.

questions.q: What is the right first aid for the speck of dust in Jovan's eye?
o: Rub the eye gently to move the speck towards the corner
Lift the speck out carefully with the corner of a clean rag
Rinse the eye with clean water or eyewash, without rubbing
Wait until the end of the shift to see if it clears
questions.why: Rubbing can scratch the eye, and trying to lift a speck out can push it in. Rinse with clean water or sterile eyewash; if it will not wash out, cover the eye and get medical help, and report it.

questions.q: What was Kimoy's pass rate this month?
o: About 76%
About 81%
About 87%
About 69%
questions.why: 13 ÷ 16 × 100 = 81.25%, about 81%. Working with the three failures instead (3 ÷ 16) gives about 19%, the fail rate.

questions.q: How should Collin deal with the three weeks that have no logbook entries?
o: Write entries for those weeks from what Kimoy remembers, and sign them
Sign the 2G task as practised, since she says she did plenty of it
Record only what he can show, and watch and record new 2G practice
Tear out the empty pages so that the gap does not show in the book
questions.why: Records must be honest: an assessor relies on them. Entries written weeks later from memory are not evidence. Collin fills the gap with new practice that he watches and records on the day.

questions.q: Why should the three failed coupons have been kept and recorded?
o: They are needed to make up the number of coupons the assessor wants
They are honest evidence of the faults she has worked on and her progress
So that the shop can re-weld them later and use them again for her final test
So that nobody else can take the steel and use it on another job
questions.why: A portfolio shows progress, not only the best pieces. Failed coupons, with what caused the fault and how it was fixed, show the assessor that the training worked.

questions.q: Kimoy asks Collin to sign her 2G unit as 'competent'. What should he tell her?
o: Yes, because as her trainer he knows her work better than anyone
Yes, but only if her pass rate stays above 80% for the whole of the month
No, because she must train for a full year before anyone signs her
The assessor judges that; his records and observations are the evidence
questions.why: A workplace trainer coaches, checks and reports. A qualified assessor makes the formal judgement of competence, using the trainer's records, the portfolio, observation and questions.

questions.q: Which change to Akeem's training is most likely to help him?
o: More short, guided practice sessions, with feedback after each run
A longer talk on welding theory at the start of every session
Moving him on to harder positions, to make the work more interesting
Stopping his training for a month so that he can catch up by himself
questions.why: Akeem improves most when he is shown again and guided while he works, so more hands-on practice in short steps, with quick feedback, suits him. More talk or harder work skips the problem.

questions.q: Which evidence would best show Mr Duhaney that the training has paid off for the shop itself?
o: Both apprentices' logbooks are neat, full and up to date
Both apprentices have asked Trevor for more training time
Fewer welds have been rejected since they joined production
Trevor has written a new and longer session plan for next year
questions.why: The owner's question is about results for the business. Fewer rejected welds and less re-work on real jobs show that the training has reached the shop's work, not only the practice booth.

questions.q: What should Trevor's report to Mr Duhaney contain?
o: Results against the objectives, gaps still left, and changes for the next plan
Only Jody-Ann's results, since they show the training at its very best
A list of the hours Trevor spent away from production while he trained them
Akeem's faults in full, so that the owner can decide whether he should let him go
questions.why: A useful evaluation report is honest and balanced: what was achieved against the plan, what still needs work, and how the next plan will change. It is about improving the training, not hiding results or blaming a trainee.

questions.q: You are demonstrating a vertical-up fillet weld with MMAW. Which electrode angle should you show?
o: Halfway between the plates, pointing slightly upwards
Pointing straight down the joint towards the floor
Square to the upright plate, at the same height as the pool
Halfway between the plates, pointing well downwards
questions.why: For vertical-up, the electrode is held halfway between the plates (about 45°) and tilted slightly upwards, about 5–15°, so the arc helps hold the pool up as it climbs. Held square to one plate, it puts the weld onto that plate; pointed well down, it lets the pool and slag run.

questions.q: Why does a bend test show faults that a visual check of the weld cannot?
o: Bending makes the weld metal harder, so faults are easier to see
Bending stretches the weld, opening hidden lack of fusion and inclusions
Bending removes the surface of the weld, so the root can be seen clearly
Bending heats the weld, so any faults inside it change colour
questions.why: A visual check sees only the surface. When the coupon is bent, any lack of fusion, slag inclusion or porosity inside the weld opens up as a crack or tear on the stretched side.
